strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem (indirect prompt injection) with a genuinely novel angle: pruning KV-cache neurons rather than modifying the prompt text or adding extra test-time LLM calls, making the method lightweight and complementary to prior prompt-engineering or workflow-based defenses.

The derivation of an upper bound on the DPO objective and its decomposition into probability and uniformity (entropy) terms provides a principled motivation for the proposed sample-efficient attribution loss, going beyond purely heuristic design.

The empirical discovery of a 'triggering effect' (that only the first one or two response tokens determine whether the model follows injected vs. user instructions) is an interesting and potentially useful observation for the broader prompt-injection literature, and is leveraged effectively to reduce sample requirements for attribution.

Reasonably thorough ablations are provided: effect of pruning ratio p, number of attributed tokens k, masking strength alpha, layer-wise distribution of pruned neurons, and transferability of learned masks between code-based and text-based attacks.

Results show consistent and often substantial reductions in attack success rate relative to simple baselines while largely preserving response quality (F1/GPT-score), across two models and three datasets/tasks.
weaknesses: The theoretical proof of Theorem 1 rests on an oddly stated and seemingly inconsistent reference-model assumption (pref(y^p|x) > pθ(y^c|x) rather than a comparison of poisoned probabilities under ref vs θ), and the argument invoking positivity of S for concavity is unnecessary since log-sigmoid is concave everywhere; this weakens confidence in the rigor of the derivation despite the conclusion likely holding under the correct assumptions.

The final attribution loss (Eq. 15) is several approximation steps removed from the theoretical bound (replacing expectations with argmax responses, then truncating to k=1 token, with Lemma 1 explicitly noted to break down in the few-sample regime), so the practical method is largely heuristic despite the theoretical framing suggesting otherwise.

Evaluation is limited to only two similarly-sized open models (LLama3-8B, Mistral-7B-Instruct) and small sample sizes (8 attribution samples, 8 test samples per dataset, 3 trials), raising concerns about generalizability and statistical robustness of the reported ASR/F1 numbers, several of which have wide variance relative to the effect size.

Baselines are restricted to simple prompt-formatting heuristics (delimiting, datamarking, base64 encoding); no comparison is made to stronger training-based (e.g., StruQ) or workflow-based (e.g., spotlighting, task shield) defenses that are cited in related work, making it hard to assess CachePrune's competitiveness against the current state of the art.

No evaluation against adaptive attackers who are aware of the defense mechanism (e.g., attacks crafted to survive neuron pruning), which is an important robustness consideration for a security-oriented defense paper.

Reproducibility details are thin: no mention of code/artifact release, and some implementation specifics (e.g., exact construction of Φ, computational cost of the attribution/pruning step) are only partially specified.

The WildChat dialogue-summarization attack setting is somewhat artificially constructed (appending a fixed instruction to induce attacks), which may not reflect realistic indirect injection scenarios and limits the ecological validity of that evaluation.
The manuscript contains numerous typographical and grammatical errors (e.g., 'trigerring effect', 'experiemnt', 'presents ai the beginning') suggesting insufficient proofreading.

strengths: The core idea is genuinely interesting: instead of modifying the prompt text or adding extra inference-time LLM calls (as prior defenses do), the paper attributes instruction-following behavior to specific neurons in the KV cache and prunes them, offering a lightweight, deployment-friendly defense compatible with context caching.

The observed 'triggering effect' (Figure 3), showing that only the first 1-2 generated tokens determine whether a response will be clean or poisoned, is an interesting empirical observation that meaningfully simplifies and motivates the proposed attribution loss.

Reasonable set of ablations are provided (effect of k, masking ratio alpha, pruning percentage p, layer-wise distribution of pruned neurons, transferability of masks across code-based vs. text-based attacks), which help build some confidence in the internal consistency of the method.
The method requires no prompt reformatting and no extra test-time LLM calls, distinguishing it from most existing baselines and making it a plausible complement to other defenses.
weaknesses: The theoretical derivation (Theorem 1) rests on an essentially unverifiable and awkwardly stated assumption about a hypothetical reference model (Eq. 19-20, where pref(y^p|x) is compared against pθ(y^c|x) rather than pθ(y^p|x), which looks like an error or at minimum needs clarification) used only to establish concavity for the Jensen's-inequality bound. This reference model then completely disappears from the final attribution loss (Eq. 9/15) and is never instantiated in the algorithm, making the DPO-derivation feel like post-hoc theoretical framing rather than a principled guide to the actual method.

Empirical evaluation is narrow: only two 7-8B models (LLama3-8B, Mistral-7B) and three datasets are tested, with all attacks following a similar random-position context-injection paradigm from a single prior benchmark (Abdelnabi et al., 2024). No adaptive-attacker or stronger/adversarially-optimized injection is evaluated, and no larger or closed-source model is tested despite the KV-cache pruning method inherently requiring white-box access (a limitation that is never explicitly discussed).

Baseline comparison is weak: the paper deliberately excludes fine-tuning/preference-based defenses (e.g., StruQ, which is cited but not compared) and only compares against simple prompt-engineering heuristics (delimiting, datamarking, base64 encoding). This makes it hard to judge how CachePrune stacks up against the current best practical defenses, even though the stated motivation (efficiency) does not preclude such comparisons being included for context.
Standard deviations across 3 trials are reported only for CachePrune, not for any baseline, so the claimed improvements over baselines cannot be assessed for statistical significance.

The attribution procedure uses only N=8 samples from a small held-out pool of 400 prompts; the paper claims 'sample efficiency' but never empirically compares against attribution with larger N or shows a sample-efficiency curve to substantiate this specific claim.

The 'triggering effect' construction for the attribution loss injects an artificial instruction ('Answer this at the end.') to force the model into a particular failure mode during attribution — this handcrafted intervention somewhat undercuts the claim that the approach relies purely on the LLM's 'own' distinction between data and instruction, and it is unclear how sensitive results are to this specific construction.

The write-up has numerous typos and unpolished phrasing throughout (e.g., 'perference', 'trigerring', 'undersdanding', inconsistent notation such as switching between L and calligraphic L, H used for both entropy and hidden states), which reduces clarity and reproducibility confidence.

Details needed for reproducibility are incomplete or inconsistent, e.g., exact test-set sizes for SQuAD/HotpotQA/WildChat splits, full specification of the GPT-Judge prompt/protocol, and precise description of how pruning of the KV cache interacts with multiple downstream queries over the same cached context are not fully spelled out.

strengths: Novel and practically appealing idea: instead of modifying the prompt or adding extra test-time LLM calls, the method identifies and prunes a small set of task-triggering neurons directly in the KV cache, making it compatible with context caching and imposing no extra inference-time computation.

The method is grounded in a principled derivation: an upper bound of the DPO objective is derived (Theorem 1) and connected to the proposed attribution loss (Lemma 1), providing some theoretical motivation for the design choices rather than purely heuristic engineering.

The 'triggering effect' observation (Figure 3) — that only the first one or two response tokens determine whether the model treats context as data or instruction — is an interesting empirical finding that meaningfully improves sample efficiency of the attribution procedure (only N=8 samples needed).

Reasonably thorough ablation studies are provided: effect of k (number of attributed tokens), pruning ratio p, masking strength α, layer-wise distribution of pruned neurons, and transferability of the learned mask across code-based vs. text-based attacks.

Experimental results show consistent ASR reductions relative to prompt-engineering baselines while largely preserving response quality (F1/GPT-score), across two different model families (LLama3-8B, Mistral-7B) and three tasks/datasets.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to only two moderately sized open-weight models (7-8B) and no larger or closed-source models are tested, limiting evidence that the approach scales or generalizes across architectures/sizes.

Effectiveness is inconsistent across settings: e.g., ASR on HotpotQA with LLama3-8B remains fairly high after defense (15.23%), and improvements are noticeably weaker there than on SQuAD or with Mistral, without much discussion of why or how this could be mitigated.

Comparisons exclude training-based or workflow-based defenses (StruQ, task-shield, etc.) on grounds of 'fairness,' but this leaves the paper without evidence of how CachePrune compares to the field's stronger baselines, only against relatively weak prompt-formatting heuristics.

No evaluation against an adaptive or attack-aware adversary who knows the defense mechanism (e.g., an attacker crafting injections specifically to survive neuron pruning); without this, the robustness claims are somewhat narrow.

Sample sizes used for evaluation appear small (attribution with N=8 samples per prompt, and only 8 prompts sampled per dataset for some settings) and it is not entirely clear from the text how large the actual test sets for ASR/F1 computation are, raising some reproducibility and statistical-robustness concerns despite reported variances.

The reduction from the full expectation-based attribution loss to a single most-probable-token heuristic, and the choice of pruning percentage p and threshold Φ, rely on intuitive justifications rather than tight theoretical guarantees, so the practical algorithm departs non-trivially from the theory in Section 2.3.
Minor clarity/writing issues (typos such as 'trigerring', 'experiemnt', 'undersdanding') and some notation inconsistencies that could confuse readers trying to reproduce the method precisely.

strengths: Novel and practically appealing defense mechanism: identifying and pruning 'task-triggering' neurons directly in the KV cache to enforce a data/instruction distinction, without altering the prompt text or requiring extra LLM calls at test time, making it compatible with context caching in production LLM APIs.

Extensive empirical evaluation across three different LLMs (LLama3-8B, Mistral-7B, Phi-3.5-mini) and three task settings (SQuAD, HotpotQA, WildChat dialogue summarization), with multiple complementary metrics (ASR, F1, ROUGE-1/2/L, BERTScore, GPT-judge score) that largely corroborate each other.

Thorough ablation studies examining the effect of the number of attribution samples (N), the triggering-token window (k), the masking strength (α), the pruning ratio (p), and the importance of the selective thresholding subset Φ, which help validate design choices.

Additional robustness analyses beyond the main results, including transferability of learned masks across different attack instructions and across code-based vs. text-based injections, and a dedicated adaptive-attack evaluation using GCG-style optimization against the defense itself.

The 'triggering effect' observation (that a poisoned vs. clean response can be determined by only the first one or two generated tokens) is an interesting empirical finding that meaningfully improves sample efficiency of the proposed attribution procedure.
Method requires very few samples (N=8) and a single forward pass, making it far cheaper than fine-tuning-based or multi-call test-time defenses, which is a genuine practical advantage.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification (Theorem 1 and Lemma 1 relating the proposed loss to an upper bound of DPO) rests on a strong and somewhat circular assumption about the reference model (pref(y|x) > pθ(y|x) for both clean and poisoned responses simultaneously) that is not well motivated, and the Jensen's inequality argument's concavity condition depends on this assumption holding a priori; overall this derivation reads more as a heuristic motivation than a rigorous guarantee.

The threat model assumes the context/instruction boundary (cs, ce) is known at test time, which restricts applicability to settings with fixed API templates; while the paper argues this is common in prior work, it is a nontrivial limitation not deeply discussed in terms of failure modes when boundaries are ambiguous or adversarially obfuscated.

Comparisons are limited to prompt-engineering baselines (Delimiting, Datamarking, Sandwich, Encode_Base64); no direct quantitative comparison to competitive training-based (StruQ, SecAlign) or workflow-based (Task Shield, Spotlighting) defenses is provided, even though these are discussed qualitatively, leaving open how CachePrune compares in absolute effectiveness against state-of-the-art defenses.

The adaptive attack analysis, while a good-faith effort, only explores GCG-style token insertion against the attribution loss and does not consider an attacker with white-box knowledge of exactly which neurons/positions are pruned, which would be a stronger and more realistic adaptive threat given the method's mechanism is now public.

Evaluation is restricted to QA-style tasks and one summarization dataset with an artificially inserted trigger phrase to increase attack difficulty; generalization to more diverse, naturally occurring injection scenarios (e.g., tool-use agents, web content, multi-turn dialogues) is not tested.

Results rely on only 3 trials with small sample-based attribution (N=8), and while standard deviations are reported, no formal significance testing is conducted; some gains over the strongest baselines (e.g., Datamarking) are numerically modest in certain settings (e.g., HotpotQA on LLama3-8B).

Minor presentation issues, including apparently miscited 'Anonymous' references for related defense papers, and some imprecise/informal claims (e.g., speculative explanation about logarithms 'distorting' attribution scores) that are not empirically substantiated.

strengths: The core idea—identifying and pruning 'task-triggering' neurons directly in the KV cache via a lightweight attribution procedure—is a reasonably novel angle on indirect prompt injection defense that avoids extra test-time LLM calls or prompt reformatting, and is explicitly compatible with context-caching APIs, which is a genuine practical advantage over test-time workflow defenses.

The empirical evaluation is fairly extensive: three different LLMs (LLaMA3-8B, Mistral-7B, Phi-3.5-mini), three datasets/tasks (SQuAD, HotpotQA, WildChat summarization), several prompt-engineering baselines, and numerous ablations (k, N, p, alpha, with/without Φ, layer-wise neuron distribution, mask transferability across attack types).

The authors go beyond the main ASR/F1 table with meaningful robustness checks, including an adaptive GCG-style attack (Appendix G) and additional evaluation metrics (ROUGE-1/2/L, BERTScore) to address concerns about F1 as a sole quality proxy in free-form generation, which strengthens confidence in the reported gains.

An attempt is made to theoretically motivate the simplified preferential attribution loss by relating it to an upper bound of the DPO objective (Theorem 1, Lemma 1), providing some principled grounding for an otherwise heuristic design choice.
weaknesses: The method fundamentally assumes the context/instruction boundary (cs, ce) is known at inference time; while the authors argue this matches fixed-template API settings, it substantially narrows the claimed generality of the defense and should be more prominently reflected in the framing and limitations rather than treated as a minor caveat.

Key components feel ad hoc and under-justified: the subset Φ in Eq. (11) uses an arbitrary factor of 2 with no principled derivation beyond an ablation showing it helps; the choice to drop the logarithm in the attribution loss is justified only by a one-sentence 'suspicion' deferred to future work; and the triggering-effect mechanism relies on artificially prepending 'Answer this at the end' to construct the poisoned response for attribution, which is a attack-format-specific trick whose generality to other injection styles is not well established.

The main results are not uniformly superior: on HotpotQA with Phi-3.5, CachePrune's F1(attack) (9.79) is worse than Delimiting (11.11); on WildChat with LLaMA3, GPT-Score is essentially tied with Vanilla (3.32 vs 3.32) despite ASR gains, undercutting the claim that quality is never compromised.

The comparison set is restricted to relatively dated/simple prompt-engineering baselines (Delimiting, Datamarking, Sandwich, Encode_Base64); no empirical comparison (even as a contextualizing reference point) is made against stronger training-based or structured-query defenses (e.g., StruQ, Jatmo) that are discussed in related work, making it hard to judge CachePrune's absolute competitiveness.

The adaptive-attack results are inconsistent across models (near-complete success on LLaMA3 baselines but much weaker on Mistral/Phi-3.5), and the explanation offered ('smoother embedding landscape') is speculative and not verified, leaving open whether CachePrune's apparent adaptive-robustness generalizes or is partly an artifact of attack optimization difficulty on certain models.

Reproducibility is complicated by the density of heuristic hyperparameters (p, α, k, N, Φ threshold) and by reliance on greedy approximate positive/negative sampling (Appendix E) whose sensitivity to prompt perturbation choices is not deeply analyzed; many critical implementation details are relegated to appendices, making the main text alone insufficient to reproduce results.

strengths: The core idea—identifying and pruning 'task-triggering' neurons in the KV cache of the context span—is a genuinely novel and lightweight defense that avoids prompt reformatting and extra test-time LLM calls, distinguishing it from most prior work in this space.

The preferential attribution loss is motivated by a formal (if loose) connection to DPO, including a derived upper bound and asymptotic consistency lemma (Theorem 1, Lemma 1), giving some theoretical grounding beyond a purely heuristic design.

The 'triggering effect' observation (Figure 3) that only the first token(s) of generation determine clean vs. poisoned trajectories is an interesting empirical finding that meaningfully improves sample efficiency (N=8) and is well illustrated.

Extensive experimental coverage: three different LLMs, three datasets (SQuAD, HotpotQA, WildChat), multiple quality metrics (F1, ROUGE-1/2/L, BERTScore, GPT-judge), several ablations (k, α, N, pruning ratio p, subset Φ), transferability studies across attack types and injection modalities, and an adaptive GCG-based attack evaluation—this breadth substantially strengthens the empirical case.

Results show consistent and often large reductions in ASR while largely preserving or even improving response quality relative to strong prompt-engineering baselines, and the paper appropriately flags Encode_Base64 as an unfair comparison due to its quality degradation.
Reasonable reproducibility support: baseline definitions, evaluation code snippets, and appendix details on sampling procedures and prompts are provided.
weaknesses: The method requires pre-known context/instruction boundaries, which the paper acknowledges but which meaningfully limits applicability outside API-templated settings; this constraint deserves more prominent discussion of real-world impact rather than being confined to a brief related-work remark.

Several citations in the Related Works section reference 'Anonymous, 2024a/b/c' papers—this is unusual and raises a possible double-blind review policy concern (e.g., citing under-review anonymous work, potentially self-citations) that should be clarified/resolved.

The theoretical justification (Theorem 1, Lemma 1) mainly establishes qualitative sign-consistency/asymptotic behavior between the attribution loss and the DPO upper bound; it does not rigorously justify that the specific simplified loss (probability without log, single most-probable samples) is a good finite-sample approximation, so the theory functions more as a plausibility argument than a tight guarantee.

Sample efficiency claims rest on very small N (default 8, tested up to 12); while ablations show relative stability, the standard deviations in several tables (e.g., adaptive attack, N ablation) are non-trivial relative to the effect sizes, raising some concern about the robustness of specific numeric conclusions across seeds/samples.

The WildChat evaluation setup involves an artificially inserted instruction ('You should primarily focus on this question') to induce attackable behavior, which is a somewhat contrived scenario and provides a weaker test of ecological validity compared to the QA-based settings.

No comparison against training-based or workflow-based defenses is included in the main results (justified by compute cost, but this leaves open how CachePrune's efficacy compares against the strongest known defenses in absolute terms, even if compute is not commensurable).
